newsitem.title: USA: RTRS - FOCUS - Advertising - more venues, targeted ads.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - FOCUS - Advertising - more venues, targeted ads.

text.p: Advertising on the Internet has reached an estimated $200 million on an annualized basis, and analysts said Thursday they see that figure growing as the industry matures.
"It will be a very real part of people's budgets," Merrill Lynch analyst Lauren Rich Fine said at the Association of National Advertisers Inc.'s annual television advertising forum.
Advertisers in the near future will have myriad venues to reach consumers, making it easier to tailor their message but more difficult to choose where and how to push it.
A panel of analysts said that the growing number of households with access to the Internet presents an opportunity to meld a variety of advertising forums.
Conceivably, a household could end up with a single device that would be used to pay bills, access the Internet, watch television and provide telephone service.
The information gleaned as consumers meander through the Internet will allow advertisers to target an audience they know has already shown an interest in their type of product.

That could be done in an unobtrusive way that would offer more assurances than traditional media -- broadcasting and print -- that the advertising would actually reach consumers, Merrill Lynch's Fine said.

While readers can turn the page on a newspaper ad or can step away from the television set while an ad is airing, a computer user would be more likely to spot a small ad that popped up on their screen.
"It's not considered intrusive. It's not getting in the way of anything you're doing," Fine said.
Based on a review of fourth quarter results from America Online Inc. and other Internet providers, Fine estimated about $200 million in annualized advertising currently.
Fine considers that a "fairly tremendous" increase in just a few years.
It remains uncertain, however, how the media industry will be shaped in coming years.
Analysts said while the industry currently was fragmented, they expected it will eventually undergo a period of consolidation.

It would not be an efficient way to advertise "until we get a reconsolidation," Sanford Bernstein & Co. analyst Tom Wolzien said. "Ten years out, my guess is, you'll see a consolidation out to six guys."
Until then, however, it remains a complicated formula for advertisers. While in the past there were a limited number of forums among which to choose for advertising, the choices are growing rapidly.
"That is a much more complex environment than today," Smith Barney analyst John Reidy said.
